items.rationale: The model keeps nothing between calls; the program holds the conversation as a list and sends it again each time. Thinking the model or a provider session remembers it shows the idea that memory is automatic.

Call 1 sends 1,000 + 100 = 1,100 tokens. Call 2 sends all of that plus the 50-token tool request and the 450-token result: 1,600. Total 1,100 + 1,600 = 2,700. Answering 1,600 forgets that call 1 is billed too; 1,650 counts only one call's history.

The chunk lost the context saying which machine it is about, so the fix is to restore it by prepending a short chunk-specific note before indexing (contextual retrieval). Returning more chunks, a bigger prompt or a larger window adds cost without making this chunk identifiable.

The memory tool is client-side: the model only requests a file operation, and the application executes it against storage the developer controls. Answering the model shows the misconception that the model carries out the action itself.

Stale tool results are the cheapest thing to drop, and the program controls the history, so it can delete them and leave a stub. The model has no saved memory to store (b), restarting loses the work (c), and an instruction to pay less attention still sends and bills the tokens (d).
